meta.description: Descartes never wrote "Doubt is the origin of wisdom." Wikiquote lists it as misattributed — the Latin surfaces in an 1880 footnote, not his works.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Doubt is the origin of wisdom'?
meta.ogDescription: The pithy Latin maxim pinned on Descartes isn't in his writings. Here's what he actually wrote about doubt — and where the line really comes from.

answer.label: Not René Descartes — an unsourced Latin maxim
answer.authorDates: Origin undocumented · a maxim wrongly pinned on Descartes
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Descartes, even dressed up in Latin as “Dubium sapientiae initium,” but the line appears in none of his works. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed ↗: the Meditations often cited as its source does not contain it, and the Latin instead turns up in a footnote to the 1880 edition of Publilius Syrus’ Sententiae. The idea of doubt-before-knowledge is authentically Cartesian; this exact aphorism is not.

source.excerpt: Dubium sapientiae initium. — “Doubt is the origin of wisdom.”
trail: Wikiquote places the line in its Misattributed section ↗, noting no original source supports it and that the Meditations sometimes cited does not contain it.
Popular quote sites cement the error — Goodreads attributes it to Descartes, ‘Meditations on First Philosophy’ ↗, a citation that does not check out.
What Descartes did write about doubt is longer: ‘…at least once in your life you doubt, as far as possible, all things’ ↗ — Principles of Philosophy, Part 1, Art. 1 (1644).
source.excerptNote: A Latin maxim widely captioned as Descartes; it is absent from his published writings.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording cannot be tied to any datable work by Descartes; per Wikiquote ↗ the Latin form surfaces only in a footnote to an 1880 edition of Publilius Syrus, so its true authorship and first publication are undocumented. With the origin unknown, no copyright status can honestly be asserted.

author.name: René Descartes
author.heading: René Descartes
author.metaLine: 1596–1650 · French philosopher, mathematician & founder of modern rationalism
author.bio: René Descartes made systematic doubt the engine of his philosophy: in the Meditations (1641) and Principles of Philosophy (1644) he resolved to set aside everything that could possibly be doubted in order to reach an indubitable foundation — famously arriving at cogito, ergo sum. Because doubt is so central to his method, feel-good one-liners about doubt gravitate to his name. But the tidy maxim “Doubt is the origin of wisdom” is a later coinage he never wrote; what he actually wrote is longer, more careful, and about method rather than aphorism.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented as a Descartes attribution in modern quote collections; per Wikiquote, “René Descartes” (Misattributed), the Latin “Dubium sapientiae initium” appears in a footnote to Publilii Syri mimi Sententiae (1880 ed.), not in Descartes. Genuine parallel: Descartes, Principles of Philosophy (Principia Philosophiae), Part 1, Art. 1 (1644).

misattribution.heading: Why this one is misattributed
misattribution.intro: “Doubt is the origin of wisdom” is a textbook magnet quote: a clever, self-improving one-liner welded to a famous thinker whose actual subject was doubt. The Latin dress makes it look primary-sourced, but the citation collapses on inspection.

items.why: Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ states plainly that no original source supports the attribution, and that the Latin “Dubium sapientiae initium” appears not in Descartes but in a footnote to the 1880 edition of Publilius Syrus’ Sententiae.
Quote databases such as Goodreads ↗ pin the line to the Meditations, but the phrase does not occur there — the citation is repeated, not verified.

misattribution.truthLine: Descartes championed methodical doubt, but his real formulation reads: ‘If you would be a real seeker after truth, it is necessary that at least once in your life you doubt, as far as possible, all things’ ↗ (Principles of Philosophy, Part 1, Article 1, 1644) — not the bumper-sticker “Doubt is the origin of wisdom.”

context.heading: The idea is his; the sentence isn't
lead: Descartes really did make doubt the starting point of knowledge. His method was to treat as false anything that could be doubted, stripping belief down to what survives — the move that yields cogito, ergo sum. So attributing a doubt-praising maxim to him feels right, which is exactly why the misattribution sticks.

But “consistent with his philosophy” is not the same as “written by him.” The compact aphorism, and even its Latin form, trace to no Cartesian text; the earliest thread anyone has found runs instead to a 19th-century edition of a Roman sententiae collection.
context.pull: Descartes prized doubt — but he never wrote this sentence about it.
